# From map to scene

The editor never writes Godot scenes itself. It saves a `.gtm` file, and the addon turns that file into nodes. This page covers the ways that happens, from a manual build to hot reloading a game that is already running.

## Building a map

A `FuncGodotMap` node does the work. Give it a map with *Local Map File*, a `res://` path to a `.gtm`, `.map` or `.vmf`, or with *Global Map File* for a file outside the project, which wins when both are set. *Map Settings* falls back to the project's `func_godot/default_map_settings`. **Build Map** generates everything and **Clear Map** removes it.

A build clears the node's children, then turns brushes into meshes and collision, creates the entities and applies their properties, and connects every entity's outputs. Terrain, scatter, the environment from worldspawn and the chunk streamer come last, and the node emits `build_complete` when it is done.

The built nodes are owned by the scene. A map built in the editor is saved into the `.tscn` and loads like any other scene, and nothing is rebuilt at runtime unless you ask. You can still build from code, which is how the demo's scripted scene works:

cards.code:
var map := FuncGodotMap.new()
map.map_settings = load("res://demo/demo_map_settings.tres")
map.local_map_file = "res://demo/maps/scripted_scene.gtm"
add_child(map)
map.build()

## Materials and how big a texture looks

A face's material is a path under the texture folder without its extension, such as `showcase/planks`. When a material file with that name sits next to the image, `showcase/planks.tres` here, the build uses it as it is, and the editor previews the same file, so transparency, emission and normal maps look alike on both sides. Without one the addon makes a plain material from the image.

UVs count texels, and a texel is normally one pixel of the image, which means a 64 pixel texture repeats every 64 map units, two meters at the default scale. That is right for pixel art and wrong for photos, where a 1024 pixel scan of a two meter wall would stretch across thirty meters. A material can state how much of the world one repeat covers with its `texture_size` metadata, in map units, and from then on the editor and the build divide by that instead of the pixel count. Faces, displacements, decals, the Texture tool and UV editor, fit and justify all follow it, and swapping an image for a sharper one no longer changes the map.

You can add the metadata in Godot's inspector as well, under *Metadata*, as a `Vector2` or a single number for a square repeat. Terrain layers keep their own `tile` setting, which already measures the repeat in map units. The demo project's textures are CC0 photo scans from Poly Haven and ambientCG, each material set to the real size of its scan, and `tools/fetch_demo_textures.py` in the repository rebuilds them along with a list of their sources.

A material glows when its file sets `emission_enabled`. Godot adds the emission texture to the emission color and multiplies the sum by `emission_energy_multiplier`, or multiplies color and texture when `emission_operator` is 1, so with the default black color a texture glows exactly as painted. Without a material file, an image named like the albedo with `_emission` added becomes the glow map of the generated material. Emissive materials carry a glow badge in the Materials panel, and the lit view adds their light before tone mapping, which keeps a neon sign bright on a dark street. Decals, blends and terrain layers keep the glow of the materials they are made from.

Night maps set the sky from worldspawn: a dim, pale blue sun stands in for the moon, `ambient_energy` and `sky_energy` darken the ambient light and the sky, `glow_intensity` makes lamps and emissive surfaces bloom in Godot, and `ssr` set to 1 turns on screen space reflections so wet streets and puddles mirror them. Lights take a `shadows` key, and a light's `fixture` key names the glowing bulb or tube that belongs to it, which then goes dark or disappears whenever the light is off, see the lights in [[entity-reference]]. The night district in `examples/mcp/night_district.json` is a complete night map built this way, its street lamps, wall lamps and hall tubes all wired through `fixture` instead of manual outputs, from lit windows to a flickering alley lamp. The withered city in `examples/mcp/withered_city.json` goes further into neon: a wet street of blade and box signs made of block letters, glowing paper lanterns, and a storm whose lightning bolt is the fixture of a light a random timer flashes.

## Rebuild on save

While the Godot editor is open, the addon runs a small server called the live link, on port 7842 by default. When you save in GodotTrench, the editor tells Godot, and Godot rebuilds every `FuncGodotMap` **in the scene you have open** whose file matches and whose *Auto Rebuild On Save* is on, which it is by default. Maps in other scenes are left alone until you open them and build.

The editor's status bar reports what happened: how many map nodes were rebuilt, that no open scene uses the map, or that no Godot with the addon answered. A rebuild marks the scene as modified, so save it in Godot to keep the result.

*Godot > Live Mode* goes a step further and streams edits into that scene before you save. It needs the map to have been saved once, and like rebuild on save it only touches the scene open in the Godot editor.

## Hot reload in a running game

To see changes in a game that is already running, register the hot reload script as an autoload under *Project Settings > Globals > Autoload*:

It listens on port 7843, rebuilds the matching maps whenever you save, and then emits `map_reloaded(map)`, which is your chance to put the player back at a spawn point or reset game state. It only runs in games launched from the Godot editor, unless you set `enabled_in_exported_builds` on it.

> [!WARNING] Every rebuild frees what is under the map
> A manual build, a rebuild on save and a hot reload all start by deleting the map node's children. A player or pickup you parented under the map node disappears with them. Keep your own nodes beside the map node, or put them in an overlay as described next.

## Godot overlays

Some things belong to the game rather than the level: a vending machine with its own script, a particle effect you tuned in Godot, a sign, a lamp with an AnimationPlayer. You still want them in the same place as the map and you do not want to lose them every time the map is rebuilt. That is what an overlay is for. Add a `GodotTrenchOverlay` node as a direct child of the `FuncGodotMap` and put your nodes under it. Builds, Clear Map, rebuilds on save, live mode and hot reload all skip it, so its nodes stay the same instances with the same owner, signals and state, and it is saved with your scene like anything else you made. After the next build it is listed first under the map, before the generated nodes.

Overlay content lives in the map's own space and is measured in meters, the same as the generated nodes. With the default scale of 32 units per meter, a child at `(2, 0, -3)` sits where GodotTrench shows `(64, 0, -96)`. The overlay itself always stays at the map origin, so moving the map moves everything on it. An overlay kept somewhere else in the scene can point at its map with *Map Path* and follows the map's transform instead, and for a single node there is a lighter option: a direct child of the map in the `godottrench_keep` group survives builds as well.

### Wiring an overlay to the map

Overlay nodes take part in the map's inputs and outputs. To let a map output reach one, give it a `GodotTrenchOverlayIO` child and set its *Targetname*. From then on the node behaves like an entity with that name: an input calls its method of the same name, sets its property of the same name to the parameter, or runs one of the built in inputs such as `show`, `hide` or `toggle`. That is enough for nodes without a script, since an output with input `emitting` and parameter `true` starts a `GPUParticles3D`. The component also emits `input_received(input, parameter, activator)` for every input it gets, which you can connect to anything in the editor.

The other direction uses the same `GodotTrenchOutput` nodes the build creates for entities. Add one as a child of the overlay node, pick the signal it listens to in *Output*, and fill in the target, input and parameter. An `Area3D` can fire on `body_entered` without any code, and a script can declare its own signal:

cards.code:
extends StaticBody3D
## A breaker box in the overlay. The player's use key calls use(), and GodotTrenchOutput
## children listening to flipped_on and flipped_off switch the map's lamps.

signal flipped_on(activator: Node)
signal flipped_off(activator: Node)

var on := false

func use(activator: Node = null) -> void:
	on = not on
	if on:
		flipped_on.emit(activator)
	else:
		flipped_off.emit(activator)

cards.md:
Targets are looked up by name when an output fires, so an overlay output keeps working after the entity it points at has been rebuilt, and a map output finds overlay nodes the same way it finds entities. A rebuild does reset the map, though: entities come back in their starting state while the overlay keeps its own, so a switch that was on still says on while its lamps are off. The overlay emits `map_rebuilt(map)` after every build, and that is the moment to send your state back to the map.

Some content should stay on an entity rather than on the map, like a warning plate on a roller door. Put it under a `GodotTrenchAnchor` and set *Target* to the entity's targetname. The anchor binds at the offset where you placed it, then follows the entity when a rebuild or a live edit moves it and while the game moves it, so the plate goes up with the door. Moving the anchor itself changes the offset.

### What GodotTrench sees

The level editor cannot show Godot nodes, so the overlay describes itself. When the map is built in the Godot editor and whenever the scene is saved, it writes a small `<map>.overlay.json` next to the map with the name, bounds and targetnames of each of its direct children. GodotTrench reads that file and draws each child as a dashed blue ghost box with its name, so a level designer can see where the breaker box stands before building a wall through it. *View > Godot Overlays* hides them. Overlay targetnames also count as real targets: the Issues panel no longer reports outputs aimed at them as missing, and they show up in the target list of the output editor. Turn off *Share With Editor* on an overlay to keep it out of the file.

The night district in the demo project comes with an overlay, `demo/overlays/night_district_overlay.tscn`. Its breaker box switches the map's courtyard lamps, the map's courtyard trigger turns on its string lights and fireflies, steam rises from a manhole, and a keep clear plate rides the warehouse roller door.

## The debug overlay

Add a `GodotTrenchDebugOverlay` node to your scene and press F3 in the running game. It lists outputs as they fire and draws every trigger volume, which answers the usual question of why a door did not open: either the trigger never fired, or it fired at a target that does not exist. The volumes are collected at the moment you turn the overlay on, so toggle it again after spawning new triggers. (F3 in the editor is Lit Preview, which is unrelated.)

For logging from code, `GodotTrenchIO.events()` returns an object whose `fired(source, output, target, input, parameter)` signal is emitted for every output, including ones whose target resolves to nothing. That makes it the most reliable way to catch a silent wiring mistake.

## Streaming big maps

Large outdoor maps can stream their visuals by distance. Select nothing in the editor so the Inspector shows worldspawn, and set `chunk_streaming` to 1. `chunk_size`, 2048 units by default, sets the size of a cell, and `load_radius`, 8192 by default, how far from the camera cells stay visible. The build splits oversized meshes into cells and shows or hides them as the camera moves.

Streaming only hides meshes. Collision and scripts keep running across the whole map, so it saves rendering cost, not physics or logic. The streamer node emits `area_loaded(key, bounds)` and `area_unloaded(key, bounds)` if you want to stream your own content alongside it.

## The game config in more detail

`godottrench_game.json` is how the editor learns about your project. It is written by the `GodotTrenchGameConfig` resource named in the `godottrench/game_config` project setting, and contains every class from that config's FGD with its properties, size, colour and the inputs and outputs found in its script, any C# entities, the texture folder and the unit scale.

With `godottrench/auto_export_game_config` on, the default, the addon exports again about a second and a half after Godot notices files changing. You can also export by hand from *Project > Tools*, or headless, for example in CI:

## Project settings

| Setting | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `func_godot/default_map_settings` | `res://addons/func_godot/func_godot_default_map_settings.tres` | Map settings for every `FuncGodotMap` that does not set its own |
| `func_godot/default_inverse_scale_factor` | 32 | Map units per meter |
| `godottrench/game_config` | `res://addons/func_godot/game_config/godottrench/godottrench_game_config.tres` | The config resource that writes `godottrench_game.json` |
| `godottrench/auto_export_game_config` | true | Export again when files change |
| `godottrench/live_link_enabled` | true | Run the live link server in the Godot editor |
| `godottrench/live_link_port` | 7842 | Must match the port in the editor's preferences |
| `godottrench/threaded_build` | true | Use the WorkerThreadPool for brush conversion and mesh building |
| `godottrench/live_chunk_size` | 16.0 | In live mode, split worldspawn into chunks of this many meters, only rebuild changed chunks |
| `godottrench/csharp_entity_dirs` | `res://` | Where C# entities are found at build time |
